newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian c. bank warns against printing money.
newsitem.headline: Russian c. bank warns against printing money.

text.p: Russia's central bank warned the State Duma lower house on Tuesday that issuing extra money would trigger inflation, and speed up the fall in production, but not raise liquidity in the economy.
"The consequences (of such a step) will undermine the Russian economy," it said in a statement.
Last week some deputies in a conciliation commission set up to iron out the 1997 draft budget suggested printing money to cover the budget deficit.
Communist Party and Agrarian deputies suggested raising the ratio of money to gross domestic product to 21 percent from the current 12.5 percent. The suggestion did gain enough votes to be approved.
The central bank said this step would result in a year-on-year inflation rate of 180-270 percent in the first nine months of 1997.
The fall in inflation, to 1.2 percent a month in October from 17.8 percent in January 1995, is one of the government's main achievements. The year-on-year rate in October was 27.2 percent.
But money is scarce, making it hard for companies and the government to pay its bills, contributing to a widespread non-payments crisis in the economy.
The central bank said the depreciation of the rouble would lag behind the inflation rate, leading to heavier capital flight and massive purchases of dollars by households.
Capital flight from Russia has amounted to between $60 and $80 billion since the start of economic reforms in 1992.
High inflation would result in a depreciation of the country's assets and lead to falling demand and a more rapid decline in industrial output, the bank said.
However, the measures would not raise liquidity because high inflation would push the ratio of M2 to gross domestic product to five-six percent, it said.
The Central Bank law prohibits the government from taking direct credits from the central bank.
